soil-agri-224.title: Working out residue cover after tillage passes
soil-agri-224.text: Every tillage pass buries some residue, so the surface cover shrinks, and passes in sequence are estimated by multiplication. Multiply the fraction each tool leaves. For example, 80% cover after corn, then chisel (70%), tandem disk (45%), field cultivator and planter (75%) leaves about 19%. Dropping the disk leaves 42%. After corn or cereals a moldboard plough leaves 0-10% residue, twisted-point chisel 50-70%, tandem finishing disk 30-60%, field cultivator 60-90% and a row-crop planter 85-95%. Speed, depth and soil moisture affect the amounts, and cover also depends on surface roughness and soil loosening. This arithmetic shows whether a system meets the 30% threshold of {{ref:soil-agri-099}}.

soil-agri-223.title: A short history of tillage
soil-agri-223.text:
Tillage began with small-grain farmers of the Fertile Crescent, Europe and North Africa, who wanted a fine, clean seedbed. It also gave the crop a head start on weeds and stimulated mineralization of nutrients. Centuries of this system caused excessive erosion, organic matter loss and nutrient depletion, especially around the Mediterranean.

Jethro Tull's 1731 book promoted row seeding with a seed drill and intensive tillage. He believed pulverized soil particles fed plants, and he grew wheat 13 years without manure by mining soil nutrients. Pre-Columbian American farmers did differently: no full-field tillage, but direct seeding with planting sticks or hoeing small hills, with corn, beans and squash intercropped. For the practice itself, see {{ref:soil-agri-095}}.

soil-agri-225.title: Frost tillage: working soil as it freezes
soil-agri-225.text: Frost tillage means tilling soil after frost has entered it but before it has penetrated more than about 2 inches (5 cm). Water moves up to the freezing front and the soil beneath dries, and the frozen layer supports equipment, so compaction is reduced. The rough surface favours water infiltration and prevents runoff, and livestock farms can use it to incorporate or inject manure in winter. Recent research in Nebraska and Australia indicates occasional tillage does not harm soil health. Purposes include weed or insect control, incorporating immobile amendments and compaction relief. Even so, it should be rare, once every 5-10 years, with tools that leave residue, because any tillage can destroy structure built by years of {{ref:soil-agri-117}}.

soil-agri-176.title: Ridge tillage: seedbeds on raised ridges
soil-agri-176.text: Ridge tillage builds ridges or beds for the seed zone and keeps fixed traffic lanes. It is one of the conservation tillage practices ({{ref:soil-agri-099}}) that aim to keep 30% or more of the surface under crop residue, alongside no-till, in-row subsoiling and strip-till. Ridges let the seed zone dry and warm faster, give some weed control and reduce saturation after heavy rain. Fixed travel lanes reduce overall compaction. Poorly drained fields, where the {{ref:soil-water-247}} sits near the surface, benefit greatly, because the sensitive seedling root zone stays aerobic when wet (see {{ref:soil-phys-150}}).

soil-agri-217.title: Biological pest control with living enemies
soil-agri-217.text:
Sometimes the cheapest pest control is a field border. Nectar-producing plants on rice field borders cut pest densities 10- or even 100-fold, so farmers sprayed 70% less insecticide and yields rose 5%. Biological control uses other organisms to control animal pests, weeds or plant and animal pathogens. It relies on predation, parasitism and herbivory with active human management, and can be a component of {{ref:soil-agri-054}}.

Three strategies exist: importing a pest's natural enemy to a new place, augmenting by releasing more of the enemies already there, and conserving existing natural enemies. Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil-dwelling bacterium, is the most widely applied bacterial control agent, used against moth, butterfly, beetle and fly pests. It infects through the gut, so it works poorly on sucking insects.

There are risks. Some early introductions became serious pests themselves, and controls can attack native non-target species.

soil-agri-207.title: Structures or soil building: two ways to control erosion
soil-agri-207.text:
Erosion control splits into two families. Structural measures are engineered works such as terraces, diversion ditches and drop structures, which need an up-front investment. Agronomic practices change soil and crop management: reduced tillage, cover cropping and vegetating critical areas. The difference lies in timing. Structures mainly contain runoff and sediment after erosion has started, while agronomic measures prevent erosion by lowering runoff potential.

Structures cost more to build and maintain and tend to be less effective, so soil-building agronomic practices are the first choice and structures mostly complement them. Agronomic measures also improve soil health and productivity, and advances in conservation tillage machinery have shifted practice away from structures.

Both families, in the end, do one of two things. They reduce the shear forces of water and wind, or they keep soil in a condition where it cannot easily erode. See {{ref:soil-water-050}} for the wider picture.

soil-agri-204.title: Erosion's damage beyond the farm
soil-agri-204.text:
Sediment is the number one contaminant of most waters worldwide, and it often carries nutrients, pesticides and other chemicals. Soil carried off fields fills streams, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries, and blowing dust reaches towns. Off-site costs to fisheries, recreation and industry can exceed the lost farm productivity. So soil loss below T may be tolerable for yields but not for water and air quality.

Clay-rich soils are especially troublesome. Their particles stay suspended as colloids in runoff, do not settle in ponds or filter strips, and travel far with nutrients and pesticides. Clay and silt suspended in the air also travel long distances and can cause respiratory problems. This is the downstream side of {{ref:soil-water-001}}.

soil-agri-208.title: Principles of erosion control
soil-agri-208.text:
Four ideas guide most erosion control. Keep soil covered: water and wind erosion occur almost exclusively on exposed soil, and live plants protect best and stimulate soil health. Use practices that increase aggregation and infiltration, and do not disturb soil unless it is well covered, since loosening cuts runoff only briefly before the soil settles.

Focus control on high-risk spots where runoff concentrates, using inexpensive biological measures such as grass in waterways and filter strips. Also target critical periods such as after winter fallow or after the dry season. Finally, erodible fields that are not profitable may be better taken out of production under conservation reserve or set-aside payments. These build on {{ref:soil-water-050}}.

soil-agri-209.title: Reduced tillage as the top erosion fix
soil-agri-209.text:
Moving to tillage that leaves more surface cover and less disturbance is described as the single most effective way to reduce erosion. It generally pays better than conventional tillage. A rougher surface without secondary passes and packers prevents aggregate dispersion and surface sealing, cutting runoff and erosion. In an Ohio four-year test, conventional-till corn runoff averaged about 7 inches of water a year against under 0.1 inch for no-till.

Less tillage also reduces tillage erosion, which moves soil downhill and exposes subsoil on upslopes. If tillage is needed to ease compaction, use low-disturbance tools such as zone builders or strip tillers. See {{ref:soil-agri-095}} for tillage itself.

soil-agri-206.title: How farming speeds up natural erosion
soil-agri-206.text: Erosion never stops. Sahara dust carried about 3,000 miles to South America is thought to be a major phosphorus source for the Amazon basin. It is a natural geological process, but farming greatly accelerates it, especially where soil is bare. Erosion is worst when soil has no living plants, roots or residue mulch, and tillage that breaks aggregates lowers infiltration and worsens runoff. Intense or prolonged rain drives water erosion and landslides, while drought and strong winds drive wind erosion. Soils with poor aggregation, especially silts, are more susceptible, as soil erodibility ratings reflect. See {{ref:soil-water-001}}.

soil-agri-214.title: Diversion ditches: sending runoff aside
soil-agri-214.text: A diversion ditch is a channel or swale built across a slope to carry water to a waterway or pond. Its purpose is to channel water away from upslope areas, so {{ref:soil-water-019}} does not accumulate and concentrate downslope, scouring and forming gullies. A narrow filter strip on the upslope edge removes sediment.

soil-agri-216.title: Controlling landslides on farmed slopes
soil-agri-216.text: Landslides ({{ref:soil-water-057}}) are hard to control, so unstable steep slopes are best left in forest. Where steep slopes are farmed, wide-spaced trees let roots stabilize soil while leaving light for pasture or crops, as in a New Zealand poplar experiment. Horizontal drains can dewater critical zones and prevent supersaturation in long rains, but they are costly and mainly used in urban areas and along roads.

soil-agri-215.title: Wind erosion control on farmland
soil-agri-215.text: Most water-erosion controls also curb {{ref:soil-water-010}}: reduced tillage or no-till, cover crops and perennial rotation crops. A rougher surface increases turbulence near the ground and lowers wind shear, so tilled fields without cover are best left rough-tilled. Tree shelterbelts planted perpendicular to the prevailing wind reduce evaporative demand and also serve as ecological corridors that raise biodiversity.
